title: The 'barking' heart and the bitch simile
greek: κραδίη δέ οἱ ἔνδον ὑλάκτει. ὡς δὲ κύων ἀμαλῇσι περὶ σκυλάκεσσι βεβῶσα (kradiē de hoi endon hulaktei. hōs de kuōn amalēisi peri skulakessi bebōsa)
short: Watching the maids slip out to the suitors, Odysseus' heart 'barks' inside him like a bitch standing over her puppies at the sight of a stranger.
body: The verb hulaktein means 'to bark' (Murray's 'growled'). Odysseus' anger is presented as a guard-dog's: protective, fierce and instinctive, defending the household against intruders it does not recognise. Monro notes the participle 'having failed to recognise', which makes the dog in the simile react to an unknown man. The image belongs to a network of dog language in these books: the faithful hound Argos (17.291-327), the maid Melantho rebuked as a 'shameless dog' (19.91), and in the next line Odysseus' address to his heart, which has endured something 'more doglike' (kunteron) still. The simile also marks a turning point in self-control. The man who has endured kicks and missiles finds his anger hardest to hold when the household's women betray it.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.14-15

title: 'Endure, my heart'
greek: τέτλαθι δή, κραδίη· καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο ποτ᾽ ἔτλης (tetlathi dē, kradiē; kai kunteron allo pot' etlēs)
short: Striking his breast, Odysseus orders his heart to endure, recalling the Cyclops' cave: one of the most quoted lines of Homer.
body: Odysseus speaks to his heart as to a separate person, and the heart obeys: it 'remained bound' (en peisēi, 'as if moored by a cable', in Monro's explanation of the rare word peisa) while his body tossed. The comparative kunteron, literally 'more doglike', means 'more shameful' and picks up the barking image. The example he chooses, the Cyclops eating his men while he waited for the moment to escape by craft (9.288-436), is the model of endurance leading to successful revenge. Plato quotes the lines in the Phaedo (94d-e) to show the soul ruling the body and in the Republic (3.390d, 4.441b) as an example of reason rebuking the spirited part; Monro notes an imitation by Archilochus ('Heart, my heart', fr. 128 West). The line became a model for later Greek self-address and for Stoic ideas of self-mastery.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.18 and 20.23

title: Odysseus tossing like a paunch on the fire
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε γαστέρ᾽ ἀνὴρ πολέος πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο, ἐμπλείην κνίσης τε καὶ αἵματος, ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα αἰόλλῃ (hōs d' hote gaster' anēr poleos puros aithomenoio, empleiēn knisēs te kai haimatos, entha kai entha aiollēi)
short: Sleepless, Odysseus turns from side to side like a stuffed paunch turned rapidly over a fire by a man eager for it to cook.
body: The simile is unusual and almost comic in its homeliness, and it is carefully chosen. The 'paunch full of fat and blood' is exactly the prize Odysseus won by beating Irus (18.44-9, 18.118-19), and the belly (gastēr) has been the beggar's theme throughout. Monro explains aiollei as 'makes it dance', from aiolos, 'quick-moving' or 'flickering'. The comparison works on two levels. Odysseus is like the paunch, tossed this way and that by his thoughts, and also like the cook, impatient for his business to be done. The suitors' 'graceless supper' (20.392-4) is being prepared in his mind. Few similes in Homer bring the epic hero so close to the kitchen, and the effect fits a book set almost entirely within the house.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.25 and 20.27

title: The problem of blood-vengeance
greek: εἴ περ γὰρ κτείναιμι Διός τε σέθεν τε ἕκητι, πῇ κεν ὑπεκπροφύγοιμι; (ei per gar kteinaimi Dios te sethen te hekēti, pēi ken hupekprophugoimi?)
short: Odysseus' 'harder' worry: even if he kills the suitors, where can he escape the vengeance of their families? Athena answers with confidence.
body: Homeric society had no state to punish homicide. The killer faced the vengeance of the victim's kin and usually went into exile, as Theoclymenus has done (15.272-8); Monro makes the connection here. Odysseus proposes to kill the young nobles of Ithaca and the islands at once, so the problem is enormous, and he raises it again after the slaughter (23.117-22). Athena replies by calling him schetlie ('obstinate, incorrigible', which Monro reads as half-admiring) and promising that with her beside him he could defeat fifty armed bands. The question is finally answered only at the end of the poem, when the suitors' families attack and Zeus and Athena impose an amnesty (24.413-548). The passage shows how the poem plans its ending from far off.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.41-3 and 20.45

title: 'Limb-loosening' sleep (lusimelēs)
greek: λύων μελεδήματα θυμοῦ, λυσιμελής (luōn meledēmata thumou, lusimelēs)
short: Sleep 'loosening the cares of the heart, loosening the limbs': a play on meledēmata (cares) and melea (limbs).
body: Lusimelēs, 'limb-loosening', is an old epithet of sleep and of Eros (Hesiod, Theogony 121, 911), and later of death. Monro notes that the poet here plays on the likeness between meledēmata, 'cares, anxieties', and melos, 'limb', without implying that he misunderstood the word. The two-line description marks a hinge. As Athena puts Odysseus to sleep, Penelope wakes and weeps: the couple's nights are told in counterpoint, he waking while she sleeps in Book XIX, she waking while he sleeps here, and he finally hearing her voice at dawn (20.92-4). The same language of loosening was used of the suitors' desire at the sight of Penelope (18.212) and will return when their knees give way in terror (22.68).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 20.57

title: 'Backward-flowing Oceanus'
greek: ἐν προχοῇς δὲ βάλοι ἀψορρόου Ὠκεανοῖο (en prochoēis de baloi apsorroou Ōkeanoio)
short: Penelope wishes a storm-wind would carry her off to the mouths of Oceanus, the river that encircles the world and flows back into itself.
body: In early Greek cosmology Oceanus is a great river encircling the flat earth. The epithet apsorroos, 'flowing back', describes its circular course, returning into itself (Il. 18.399; Hesiod, Theogony 776). Its streams lie at the edge of the world, near the entrance to the land of the dead (Od. 10.508-12, 11.13-22). Penelope's wish to be swept there is therefore a wish to die and vanish, as the daughters of Pandareus were snatched away (20.66-78). The precise cosmological language gives her despair a cosmic scale. Ironically, Odysseus himself has already made that journey to the edge of Oceanus and returned (Book XI).

title: The daughters of Pandareus
greek: ὡς δ᾽ ὅτε Πανδαρέου κούρας ἀνέλοντο θύελλαι ... τόφρα δὲ τὰς κούρας ἅρπυιαι ἀνηρείψαντο καί ῥ᾽ ἔδοσαν στυγερῇσιν ἐρινύσιν ἀμφιπολεύειν (hōs d' hote Pandareou kouras anelonto thuellai ... harpuiai anēreipsanto kai rh' edosan stugerēisin erinusin amphipoleuein)
short: Orphaned girls, raised by four goddesses for marriage, were snatched by the Harpies on the eve of their wedding and given to the Erinyes.
body: Penelope tells a myth known only in outline. The parents of the girls were destroyed by the gods; Aphrodite fed the orphans, Hera gave them beauty and wit, Artemis stature, Athena skill in weaving. But while Aphrodite went to Zeus to arrange their marriages, the Harpies (harpuiai, 'snatchers', Murray's 'spirits of the storm') carried them off to serve the Erinyes. Later sources fill in the crime: Antoninus Liberalis (36) makes Pandareus steal a golden dog from Zeus' sanctuary in Crete, and Pausanias (10.30.1-2) describes Polygnotus' painting of two daughters, Camiro and Clytie, at Delphi. Monro notes that this story does not obviously agree with the tale of Pandareus' daughter Aedon in 19.518-23. Penelope's use of it is clear: girls prepared for marriage and taken away just before it are her mirror, and she would rather vanish than marry 'a baser man'.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 20.66

title: Penelope's dream and Odysseus' waking impression
greek: τῇδε γὰρ αὖ μοι νυκτὶ παρέδραθεν εἴκελος αὐτῷ ... ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐφάμην ὄναρ ἔμμεναι, ἀλλ᾽ ὕπαρ ἤδη (tēide gar au moi nukti paredrathen eikelos autōi ... epei ouk ephamēn onar emmenai, all' hupar ēdē)
short: Penelope dreams that Odysseus as he was lay beside her, while Odysseus, hearing her weep, imagines that she knows him and stands at his head.
body: The night ends with a pair of near-recognitions. Penelope reports that 'a god sends evil dreams': a man like Odysseus lay beside her, and she rejoiced, thinking it waking truth (hupar) and not a dream (onar), the very contrast the eagle drew in her earlier dream (19.547). At the same moment Odysseus, hearing her voice, 'seemed in his heart' to see her standing by his head, recognising him. Monro describes this as a vivid waking impression and observes how rich the Odyssey is in words for imagination. Joseph Russo has read Books XIX and XX as a study of dream, fantasy and intuition, in which husband and wife come close to each other below the level of conscious knowledge before the recognition of Book XXIII.

sources.cite: Joseph Russo, 'Interview and Aftermath: Dream, Fantasy, and Intuition in Odyssey 19 and 20', American Journal of Philology 103 (1982) 4-18
D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.83-7 and 20.93

title: A double sign: thunder and a spoken omen
greek: φήμην τίς μοι φάσθω ἐγειρομένων ἀνθρώπων ἔνδοθεν, ἔκτοσθεν δὲ Διὸς τέρας ἄλλο φανήτω (phēmēn tis moi phasthō egeiromenōn anthrōpōn endothen, ektosthen de Dios teras allo phanētō)
short: Odysseus asks Zeus for a spoken omen from within the house and a sign outside; Zeus thunders from a clear sky and a mill-woman's words provide the other.
body: A phēmē (also called klēdōn, 18.117, 20.120) is a chance utterance that, unknown to its speaker, carries a meaning for someone else; Monro notes that neither word occurs in the Iliad. Odysseus asks for both kinds of sign at once, and both come. Zeus thunders 'from the starry sky' though 'nowhere is there any cloud', a thunderclap that can only be a portent; Monro therefore suspects the words 'out of the clouds' (20.104) as spurious, since they destroy the point. The second sign comes from the mills, where a weary woman prays that this may be the suitors' last feast. Odysseus 'rejoiced at the word of omen and at the thunder of Zeus'. The double omen sanctions the revenge from both the highest and the lowest levels of the cosmos.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.100, 20.101 and 20.104

title: The woman at the mill
greek: γυνὴ προέηκεν ἀλετρίς ... ἄλφιτα τεύχουσαι καὶ ἀλείατα, μυελὸν ἀνδρῶν (gunē proeēken aletris ... alphita teuchousai kai aleiata, muelon andrōn)
short: Twelve slave women grind barley and wheat, 'the marrow of men', through the night; the weakest, still at work, speaks the omen.
body: Grinding grain by hand was the heaviest and lowest of household tasks, done by slave women before dawn so the meal would be fresh for the day. Monro explains the details: the hand-mills 'sat' on the ground, being too heavy for any stand; alphita is barley meal and aleiata wheat flour; the woman 'stopped her mill' to speak, like Greek women of his own day who sang at the mill and fell silent when addressed. The phrase 'marrow of men' (muelon andrōn), used also at 2.290, calls bread the substance of human strength. Of the twelve women only the weakest has not finished. Her prayer that the suitors who have 'loosened her limbs with bitter labour' may eat their last meal gives a voice, briefly, to the people on whom the suitors' feasting depends.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.105-11

title: The feast of Apollo at the new moon
greek: ἐπεὶ καὶ πᾶσιν ἑορτή (epei kai pasin heortē); ἄλσος ὕπο σκιερὸν ἑκατηβόλου Ἀπόλλωνος (alsos hupo skieron hekatēbolou Apollōnos)
short: The day of the slaughter is a public festival of Apollo, the archer god, held at the new moon that the beggar had foretold.
body: Eurycleia hurries the maids because 'it is a feast-day for all'; later the heralds lead a hecatomb through the town to a shady grove of Apollo 'who shoots from afar' (20.276-8). Monro connects the festival with the new moon (noumenia), when the beggar swore Odysseus would come home 'as the old moon wanes and the new appears' (14.161-2, 19.306-7), and cites the Herodotean Life of Homer for a new-moon festival of Apollo on Samos. The choice of god is significant. Apollo is the archer, and the revenge will be accomplished with a bow, on his day; in Book XXII Odysseus prays to him before shooting Antinous (22.5-7). Norman Austin's study of the poem takes its title, Archery at the Dark of the Moon, from this conjunction.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.156 and 20.276-8 (with 14.162)
Norman Austin, Archery at the Dark of the Moon: Poetic Problems in Homer's Odyssey (Berkeley, 1975)

title: Philoetius the cowherd and the ferrymen
greek: τοῖσι δ᾽ ἐπὶ τρίτος ἦλθε Φιλοίτιος, ὄρχαμος ἀνδρῶν ... πορθμῆες δ᾽ ἄρα τούς γε διήγαγον (toisi d' epi tritos ēlthe Philoitios, orchamos andrōn ... porthmēes d' ara tous ge diēgagon)
short: The loyal cowherd brings cattle from the mainland by ferry, greets the stranger kindly and longs for his master's return.
body: Philoetius is the third herdsman to arrive, after Eumaeus and Melanthius, and the second loyal one. His cattle are kept on the mainland and brought over by ferrymen (porthmēes) 'who send other men on their way too', a rare glimpse of everyday transport. Monro notes the herds on the mainland mentioned at 14.100. Like Eumaeus he bears an honorific formula, 'leader of men', ironically applied to a slave. He greets the stranger with the same words Amphinomus used (20.199 = 18.122), weeps at the thought that Odysseus too may wander in rags, and describes his dilemma: to stay and serve the suitors, or flee abroad with the cattle. Odysseus tests him with an oath, and his answer, 'you would see what my hands can do', is fulfilled when he is told the secret (21.188-244) and kills Ctesippus (22.285-91).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.187 and 20.210-21

title: The land of the Cephallenians
greek: Κεφαλλήνων ἐνὶ δήμῳ (Kephallēnōn eni dēmōi)
short: The name for Odysseus' people as a whole; here it seems to mean the mainland territory where his cattle grazed.
body: In the Catalogue of Ships Odysseus leads 'the great-hearted Cephallenians', a name that covers the people of Ithaca, Same, Zacynthus and the opposite mainland (Il. 2.631-7). In Book XXIV Odysseus fears that the Ithacans will send messengers through the cities of the Cephallenians (24.353-5), and Laertes recalls his capture of Nericus 'on the shore of the mainland' when he ruled the Cephallenians (24.377-8). Monro notes that nothing in the Odyssey links the name with the island later called Cephallenia; here, since the cattle are on the mainland, a coastal district must be meant. The phrase reminds us that Odysseus was king of a small maritime realm, not only of one rocky island.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 20.210

title: 'No god more baneful than you, Zeus'
greek: Ζεῦ πάτερ, οὔ τις σεῖο θεῶν ὀλοώτερος ἄλλος· οὐκ ἐλεαίρεις ἄνδρας, ἐπὴν δὴ γείνεαι αὐτός (Zeu pater, ou tis seio theōn olōteros allos; ouk eleaireis andras, epēn dē geineai autos)
short: Philoetius reproaches Zeus for having no pity on the men he himself begets, borrowing a line Menelaus speaks in the Iliad.
body: The first line is identical with Menelaus' cry when his sword shatters on Paris' helmet (Il. 3.365). In the Odyssey it raises the question that the poem asks from its first scene. There Zeus complains that mortals blame the gods for evils they bring on themselves 'beyond what is fated' through their own recklessness (1.32-43). Philoetius' complaint, that the gods 'mingle' even kings with misery (Monro explains the construction as 'pity so as not to mix them with misery'), voices the opposite view from the perspective of the suffering. The poem holds both: the suitors die for their own wickedness, while good men such as Odysseus and his servants suffer for years without obvious fault. The cowherd's words prepare for the revenge as an answer to his complaint.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.195-6 and 20.203

title: The eagle on the left
greek: αὐτὰρ ὁ τοῖσιν ἀριστερὸς ἤλυθεν ὄρνις, αἰετὸς ὑψιπέτης, ἔχε δὲ τρήρωνα πέλειαν (autar ho toisin aristeros ēluthen ornis, aietos hupsipetēs, eche de trērōna peleian)
short: As the suitors plot to murder Telemachus, an eagle appears on their left carrying a dove; Amphinomus reads it as a warning and they give up the plan.
body: Birds seen on the right were favourable, those on the left unfavourable. The eagle, Zeus' bird, carrying off a weaker bird is a common type of omen in Homer: in the Iliad an eagle on the left dropping a snake causes Polydamas to warn Hector against attacking the ships (Il. 12.200-29), and in the Odyssey eagles portend the suitors' destruction (2.146-56, 15.160-78, 19.536-53). Here the sign is read correctly by Amphinomus, the most thoughtful suitor, and it saves Telemachus. But the suitors draw only half the lesson: they abandon the murder plot and go in to feast, unaware that they themselves are the doves.

title: An equal portion (moira isē) and the mean stool
greek: πὰρ δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ Ὀδυσσῆϊ μοῖραν θέσαν οἳ πονέοντο ἴσην, ὡς αὐτοί περ ἐλάγχανον (par d' ar' Odussēi moiran thesan hoi poneonto isēn, hōs autoi per elanchanon)
short: Telemachus seats his father by the stone threshold on a humble stool, but orders that he receive a share of meat equal to the suitors'.
body: The Homeric feast is a 'feast with equal shares' (dais eisē, Il. 9.225), in which each participant receives his portion (moira) as a mark of membership. Giving the beggar an equal portion therefore makes him, in principle, one of the feasters. At the same time Telemachus places him 'with crafty thought' on a mean stool at a little table by the stone threshold, which Monro identifies as the threshold of the hall entrance (17.30). The seat is humble but strategic: it is where Odysseus will stand when he begins the killing (22.1-4). Monro notes the play of words in 'having divided the portions they feasted' (dassamenoi dainunto, 20.280). Ctesippus sarcastically repeats the language of the 'equal portion, as is fitting' before throwing his ox-hoof (20.293-4).

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.257-8 and 20.280

title: Ctesippus' 'guest-gift': the ox-hoof
greek: ἀλλ᾽ ἄγε οἱ καὶ ἐγὼ δῶ ξείνιον (all' age hoi kai egō dō xeinion); βοὸς πόδα (boos poda)
short: A rich suitor from Same mocks the custom of guest-gifts by 'giving' the beggar an ox-hoof thrown at his head.
body: The xeinion is the gift a host gives a guest to seal guest-friendship (xenia), often a valuable object that will be remembered for generations (compare 1.311-18, 4.589-619). Ctesippus, 'trusting in his boundless wealth', turns the custom into an insult: his gift is an ox-hoof hurled from the basket, so that the beggar may pass it on to a bath-woman. Steve Reece's study of hospitality scenes shows how the Odyssey's many inverted or perverted receptions, of which this is one, define the suitors as violators of the most basic social bond. The poem repays the joke precisely. When the cowherd Philoetius kills Ctesippus in Book XXII, he tells him that the spear is 'a guest-gift in return for the hoof' (22.285-91).

sources.cite: Steve Reece, The Stranger's Welcome: Oral Theory and the Aesthetics of the Homeric Hospitality Scene (Ann Arbor, 1993)

anchor: a right grim and bitter smile
title: The 'sardonic' smile (sardanion)
greek: μείδησε δὲ θυμῷ σαρδάνιον μάλα τοῖον (meidēse de thumōi sardanion mala toion)
short: Odysseus dodges the hoof and smiles inwardly 'sardonically': the first appearance of the word that gives English 'sardonic'.
body: Sardanion (or sardonion) describes a bitter, grim smile or laugh. Its origin was already obscure in antiquity. Monro thinks the form sardanion has the better claim, that it must derive from a proper name that became proverbial or from a foreign word, and that the familiar explanation from a bitter herb of Sardinia, which was said to make those who ate it die with a grimace, is a later invention. Plato uses the word when Thrasymachus bursts into 'a very sardonic laugh' in the Republic (1.337a). Here the smile is internal ('in his heart'), a sign of Odysseus' self-control: he turns his head, lets the missile strike the wall, and saves his response for the right moment.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 20.302

title: 'Laughing with jaws not their own'
greek: ἄσβεστον γέλω ὦρσε, παρέπλαγξεν δὲ νόημα. οἱ δ᾽ ἤδη γναθμοῖσι γελοίων ἀλλοτρίοισιν (asbeston gelō ōrse, pareplanxen de noēma. hoi d' ēdē gnathmoisi geloiōn allotrioisin)
short: Athena stirs 'unquenchable laughter' in the suitors and drives their wits astray; they laugh with jaws not their own while their meat drips blood.
body: 'Unquenchable laughter' (asbestos gelōs) is the gods' laughter on Olympus in the Iliad (1.599); here it is a sign of madness sent by a god. Monro takes allotrioisin to mean that the laughter does not correspond to the suitors' real feeling: their faces laugh while their eyes fill with tears and 'their hearts were set on wailing'. The meat they eat seems bedabbled with blood. Monro quotes a parallel from the Icelandic Njal's Saga, in which the food on a table appears to become blood as a portent of slaughter. The scene is a collective hallucination or foreboding, felt but not understood. It turns the many laughs of the preceding books into horror, and opens the way for Theoclymenus' vision.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.347-9 (with the Njal's Saga parallel from Butcher and Lang)

anchor: Shrouded in night are your heads
title: Theoclymenus' vision of doom
greek: νυκτὶ μὲν ὑμέων εἰλύαται κεφαλαί ... ἠέλιος δὲ οὐρανοῦ ἐξαπόλωλε, κακὴ δ᾽ ἐπιδέδρομεν ἀχλύς (nukti men humeōn eiluatai kephalai ... ēelios de ouranou exapolōle, kakē d' epidedromen achlus)
short: The seer sees the suitors wrapped in night, the walls spattered with blood, the porch full of ghosts and the sun vanished from the sky.
body: Theoclymenus, descended from the prophet Melampus (15.223-56), sees the coming massacre as if present: darkness on heads and knees (death in Homer is often a darkness covering the eyes), wailing, blood on the walls and the 'fair rafters', ghosts thronging to Erebus. Monro compares 'second sight' in Celtic belief, where a shroud of mist rising up the body foretells death, and the Delphic oracle in Herodotus (7.140) that shows Athenian temples dripping blood. The last words, 'the sun has perished out of heaven', were taken by Plutarch and Heraclitus the allegorist as a description of an eclipse. Monro doubts an eclipse is meant; in 2008 Baikouzis and Magnasco argued, from other astronomical references in the poem, that the dating to the total eclipse of 16 April 1178 BC remains possible. Most literary critics read the image as the darkness of death. The suitors laugh, and the seer walks out.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.351 ff. and 20.357
C. Baikouzis and M. O. Magnasco, 'Is an Eclipse Described in the Odyssey?', Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 105 (2008) 8823-8

title: The Sicilians (Sikeloi) as slave-buyers
greek: ἐς Σικελοὺς πέμψωμεν, ὅθεν κέ τοι ἄξιον ἄλφοι (es Sikelous pempsōmen, hothen ke toi axion alphoi)
short: The suitors suggest shipping Telemachus' guests to the Sikeloi to be sold as slaves, a glimpse of the western slave trade.
body: The Sikeloi were a people of southern Italy and Sicily, the Siculi of later history. Monro suggests that in the Odyssey's world they were known to Greeks as slave-dealers, and points to the 'old Sicilian woman' who looks after Laertes on his farm (24.211, 24.366, 24.389), presumably bought from such a trade. He also reports Niebuhr's theory, based on a scholion calling Echetus 'tyrant of the Sikeloi', that the name refers to a people of Epirus, but rejects it, since Echetus is probably mythical. The suggestion shows the suitors' casual cruelty, and also the economic reality behind many of the poem's characters: Eumaeus and Eurycleia were bought, and the line between guest and saleable property is thin for those without protectors.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), note on 20.383

title: The 'graceless supper': the narrator's foreshadowing
greek: δόρπου δ᾽ οὐκ ἄν πως ἀχαρίστερον ἄλλο γένοιτο, οἷον δὴ τάχ᾽ ἔμελλε θεὰ καὶ καρτερὸς ἀνὴρ θησέμεναι (dorpou d' ouk an pōs acharisteron allo genoito, hoion dē tach' emelle thea kai karteros anēr thēsemenai)
short: Book XX ends with Penelope listening and a grim prolepsis: no supper could be less pleasing than the one a goddess and a mighty man would soon serve.
body: The narrator rarely speaks so openly about what is coming, and the effect is chilling. The suitors' midday meal is 'sweet and satisfying', but the 'supper' (dorpon, the evening meal) will be served by Athena and Odysseus, and the dishes will be death. The metaphor of slaughter as a meal is picked up when Odysseus, having strung the bow and shot through the axes, says ironically that it is time 'to prepare supper for the Achaeans' while it is still light (21.428-30). Penelope sits opposite on her chair, hearing every word in the hall (Monro discusses the arrangement in his appendix on the Homeric house). The book ends, as it began, with her and with a meal, and the last word, 'they were contriving deeds of shame', gives the moral reason for the coming punishment.

sources.cite: D. B. Monro, Homer's Odyssey, Books XIII-XXIV (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1901), notes on 20.387 and 20.392
